overview: Gaulish is the Continental Celtic language attested in roughly 800 inscriptions from pre-Roman and early-Roman Gaul (modern France, northern Italy, and surrounding regions), written between the third century BCE and the third century CE. The corpus includes monumental inscriptions, curse tablets, pottery stamps, coins, and the Coligny calendar. Study of Gaulish illuminates the archaic Celtic linguistic stage shared with Old Irish and Brittonic, provides comparative data for Indo-European reconstruction, and documents a language suppressed by Latin but preserved in epigraphy and toponymy.

alphabet.name: a
alphabet.notes: Appears in all three writing systems (Greek, Etruscan-derived Lepontic, Latin). Represents both short and long /a/, though length is not marked in inscriptions.

alphabet.name: beta / be
alphabet.notes: In Greek script represented by β; in Latin by B. Rare word-initially in native Gaulish words.

alphabet.name: ce
alphabet.notes: Latin-alphabet inscriptions use C for /k/. Greek script uses Κ κ (kappa). Before front vowels remains /k/, not palatalized as in late Latin.

alphabet.name: delta / de
alphabet.notes: Greek script δ; Latin D. Common in medial and final positions.

alphabet.name: epsilon / e
alphabet.notes: Greek script uses Ε ε. Represents both short /e/ and long /eː/. No systematic length distinction in orthography.

alphabet.name: gamma / ge
alphabet.notes: Greek script Γ γ; Latin G. Common word-initially and medially. Not palatalized before front vowels.

alphabet.name: iota / i
alphabet.notes: Greek Ι ι; Latin I. Functions as both vowel /i/ and semivowel /j/ depending on context. Length not marked.

alphabet.name: lambda / el
alphabet.notes: Greek Λ λ; Latin L. Common in all positions. Participates in consonant clusters (e.g., bl, gl).

alphabet.name: mu / em
alphabet.notes: Greek Μ μ; Latin M. Word-final -m in Latin-alphabet texts sometimes represents nasalization of preceding vowel, paralleling Old Irish treatment.

alphabet.name: nu / en
alphabet.notes: Greek Ν ν; Latin N. Assimilates in place to following consonants (e.g., /m/ before labials, /ŋ/ before velars).

alphabet.name: omicron / o
alphabet.approximation: like the o in go (without off-glide)
alphabet.notes: Greek Ο ο; Latin O. Represents both short and long /o/. Common in o-stem noun and verb morphology.

alphabet.name: pi / pe
alphabet.notes: Greek Π π; Latin P. Relatively rare word-initially due to loss of Proto-Indo-European */p/ in many Celtic environments; more common medially and in clusters.

alphabet.name: rho / er
alphabet.approximation: trilled r as in Spanish perro
alphabet.notes: Greek Ρ ρ; Latin R. Likely alveolar trill [r]. Common in all positions.

alphabet.name: sigma / es
alphabet.notes: Greek Σ σ/ς; Latin S. Does not voice to [z] intervocalically in Gaulish. Common in inflectional endings and clusters.

alphabet.name: tau / te
alphabet.notes: Greek Τ τ; Latin T. Common. In clusters with /s/ (TS) may represent an affricate [ts] or sequence [ts]; evidence ambiguous.

alphabet.name: upsilon / u
alphabet.notes: Greek Υ υ; Latin V/U (not distinguished in early Latin script). Functions as vowel /u/ and semivowel /w/. Latin V in Gaulish texts is read as /w/ in most environments.

alphabet.name: xi / ex
alphabet.notes: Greek Ξ ξ; Latin X. Represents consonant cluster [ks]. Relatively rare in native Gaulish vocabulary.

alphabet.name: chi
alphabet.approximation: like German ch in Bach, or aspirated k
alphabet.notes: Greek script only. Interpretation debated: may represent aspirated [kʰ] or fricative [χ]. Used to spell native Gaulish words with velar aspiration or lenition.

alphabet.name: theta
alphabet.approximation: like English th in thin, or aspirated t
alphabet.notes: Greek script only. May represent dental fricative [θ] or aspirated [tʰ]. Rare in Gaulish; mostly in borrowings or names.

alphabet.name: phi
alphabet.approximation: like English f, or aspirated p
alphabet.notes: Greek script only. Likely represents bilabial fricative [ɸ] or aspirated [pʰ]. Rare; used in some Greek-influenced names.

alphabet.name: omega
alphabet.approximation: long o, as in English boat (without off-glide)
alphabet.notes: Greek script only. Theoretically represents long /oː/ in contrast to omicron Ο for short /o/, but length distinction not systematically maintained in Gaulish inscriptions.

pronunciation_notes: Vowel length (short versus long vowels) was phonemic but not systematically marked in any Gaulish orthography; reconstruction depends on comparison with Old Irish and internal morphology.

The sounds written <th>, <ph>, <ch> in Greek-alphabet inscriptions are debated; they may represent aspirated stops [tʰ pʰ kʰ] or fricatives [θ ɸ χ], possibly reflecting dialectal or diachronic variation.

Word-final -m in Latin-alphabet texts may indicate nasalization of the preceding vowel rather than a true consonantal /m/, paralleling the treatment in Old Irish orthography (compare Latin accusative endings).

Gaulish preserved the Indo-European labiovelars */kʷ gʷ gʷʰ/ longer than Brittonic or Goidelic, though by the Roman period they had merged with plain velars in most dialects; some inscriptions write QU for inherited */kʷ/.
Consonant clusters are common and robust; initial clusters like /br-, dr-, gl-, tr-/ and medial clusters like /-xt-, -kt-, -mbr-/ are well attested and should be pronounced without epenthetic vowels.
Stress accent is not marked and remains uncertain; comparative evidence from Irish and Welsh suggests initial-syllable stress, but this is reconstructed, not directly attested.

grammar.noun_system: Gaulish nouns inflect for six cases (nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental), two numbers (singular, plural), and three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter). The case system is more archaic than that of the Insular Celtic languages, preserving distinctions lost in Old Irish and Old Welsh. Evidence for dual number is absent.

declensions.name: o-stem (masculine)
declensions.description: The o-stem declension, inherited from Proto-Indo-European, is the most common and best attested. Example: *mapos 'son, boy' (cf. Welsh mab, Old Irish macc).

declensions.name: ā-stem (feminine)
declensions.description: The ā-stem declension, also inherited from PIE, is common for feminine nouns and adjectives. Example: *toutā 'tribe, people' (cf. Old Irish túath, Welsh tud).

declensions.name: i-stem
declensions.description: The i-stem declension is less well attested but clearly present. Example: *turris 'tower' (Latin borrowing) and native words like *matis 'good' (adjective). Paradigm partially reconstructed from fragmentary inscriptions and comparison with Latin and Old Irish i-stems.

grammar.verb_system: The Gaulish verb system is poorly attested, with only a handful of finite forms securely identified. The language distinguished active and middle-deponent voices, at least two conjugation classes (thematic o-stem and ā-stem), and multiple tenses or aspects, though the inventory is uncertain. Mood distinctions (indicative, subjunctive, imperative) are reconstructed on comparative grounds but lack clear epigraphic confirmation in most cases. Verb-final word order is common in inscriptions.

conjugations.name: o-stem / thematic conjugation (active)
conjugations.description: The thematic conjugation is reconstructed from a small number of attested forms and comparison with Old Irish and Latin. Example: *bereti 'he carries' (cf. Old Irish ·beir, Latin fert). Only third-person forms are securely attested; other persons are reconstructed.

present_subjunctive.note: Subjunctive forms are entirely reconstructed; no clear Gaulish examples survive. Comparative method suggests forms like *berāt (3s subj.) based on Old Irish and Brittonic.

conjugations.name: middle-deponent conjugation
conjugations.description: Middle or deponent verbs, attested in a few inscriptions (notably ieuru 'I have set up/dedicated', Lezoux plate), take medio-passive endings. The form *ieuru is analyzed as 1s perfect medio-passive of *ieg- 'to set, place'. This conjugation type is parallel to Old Irish deponent verbs.

present_middle.note: Present middle forms are reconstructed from comparative evidence (Old Irish -ther, -thir endings) but not directly attested in Gaulish inscriptions. Expected forms would include *-tor (3s), *-ntori (3pl).

reading_list: Gaulish coin legends (especially DUBNO-, VERCINGETORIX, ATEKNATI): short, formulaic texts ideal for beginners; practice recognizing personal names and simple case forms.
Pottery stamps from Lezoux and Banassac (e.g., 'AVOT' genitive singular, personal names in genitive): brief, repetitive ownership or maker inscriptions; limited vocabulary but clear morphology.
The Autun spindle whorls: short flirtatious inscriptions on loom weights; trivial in scale, but the only glimpse of casual spoken Gaulish.
The Alise-Sainte-Reine inscription (RIG L-13): short votive text in Latin script; includes recognizable theonyms (god names) and dedicatory formulae.
The Chamalières lead tablet (RIG L-100): curse tablet in Latin script, ca. 100 words; connected discourse with verb forms, vocabulary of binding and magical compulsion; some gaps and obscure lexemes.
The Lezoux plate inscription (RIG L-9): short incantation or dedication in Latin script, including the verb form 'ieuru' ('I have set up'); morphology clearer than semantics.
La Graufesenque graffiti: potters' firing lists in Gaulish, distinct from the maker's stamps above; the only surviving Gaulish administrative writing.

The Coligny calendar (RIG L-III): fragmentary bronze calendar in Latin script, listing month-names and notations (MAT, ANMAT, etc.); enormous but repetitive; requires understanding of time-reckoning vocabulary and abbreviations.

The L'Hospitalet-du-Larzac lead tablet (RIG L-98): longest connected Gaulish text (ca. 160 words), curse or legal text in Latin script; complex syntax, many hapax legomena, disputed readings; advanced.
The Châteaubleau tile (discovered 1997): the longest connected Gaulish text known; its prior absence from this list was the real gap.

The Gaulish glosses in classical sources (Pliny, Dioscorides, etc.), plus Endlicher's Glossary (the Vienna glossary of Gaulish place-name elements) and Marcellus of Bordeaux's magical formulas: individual words and short formulas cited or preserved by Latin/Greek authors; useful for lexicon but limited syntax.

Cisalpine Gaulish (northern Italy, written in a north-Etruscan alphabet): the Vercelli inscription (RIG E-4, a bilingual boundary stone rather than a graffito — relabelled from the earlier description), the Todi bilingual, the Briona inscription, and the Voltino bilingual.
Lepontic (Prestino, Vergiate): earlier than and arguably a separate language from Gaulish proper; included here with that editorial caveat rather than silently omitted.

The Vercelli entry is relabelled as a bilingual boundary stone in the Cisalpine Gaulish group, not a graffito, and grouped with Todi/Briona/Voltino.
